chunks: Typical validation temperature ranges. The question: What are typical temperature ranges for validation?
Chips are sold in temperature grades that match where they will be used.
Typical ranges are 0 to 70 degrees Celsius for commercial parts, -40 to 85 degrees Celsius for industrial, and up to 125 or 150 degrees Celsius for automotive.
Engineers test chips at the cold end and the hot end, because different problems show up at each.
The real limit is the temperature of the silicon itself, which is higher than the air around it, since the chip heats itself.
Think of a hiker and the weather. A thin jacket suits mild days, a winter coat suits snow, and an arctic parka suits extreme cold. Those are the grades.
But a hiker generates heat, so the body is warmer than the air. The chip's silicon works the same way: its own temperature is the air temperature plus the heat it makes.
Bars show the ambient operating range of each grade on a common axis (the 0, 85 and 125 degrees Celsius reference lines are drawn).
Each step up in grade extends the hot end (and moves the cold end to -40 or -55 degrees Celsius), which requires more qualification and costs more.
The axis is linear from -55 to 150 degrees Celsius.
Ambient temperature: the temperature of the air around the chip. Junction temperature: the temperature of the silicon die. The physics responds to this one.
Thermal resistance ( theta JA ): how many degrees the junction warms per watt, in K/W (kelvin per watt; 1 K is a 1 degrees Celsius step).
Temperature grade: a standard range, such as commercial or industrial, that a part is guaranteed to work in. AEC-Q100: the automotive standard that defines the automotive grades.
HTOL: a long test that runs parts hot to age them quickly.
A chip dissipates 2 watts, and its package (the case around the die) has theta JA equals 30 K/W.
In a sealed box at 85 degrees Celsius, the junction reaches 85 plus 2 times 30 equals 145 degrees Celsius.
That is above a 125 degrees Celsius limit, even though the box is within the 85 degrees Celsius rating. The most this package can dissipate there is (125-85) over 30 about 1.
33 watts. With a heat sink giving 15 K/W, the junction is only 115 degrees Celsius. That is the whole idea.

"Typical grades: commercial 0 to 70 degrees Celsius, industrial -40 to 85 degrees Celsius, automotive AEC-Q100 from -40 to 85 (Grade 3) up through 105, 125 and 150 degrees Celsius (Grades 2, 1, 0), and military or space about -55 to 125 degrees Celsius.
Validation is really at junction temperature, ambient plus power times thermal resistance.
We test cold, room and hot across voltage and process corners, plus temperature cycling and high-temperature life for reliability. Exact ranges depend on the product."
